<problem>
Let \(\mathbb C_7\) be the completion of an algebraic closure of \(\mathbb Q_7\), with valuation \(v_7(7)=1\). For each integer \(r\geq1\), let \(\mathcal O_r=W(\mathbb F_{7^r})\) be the ring of integers in the unramified extension of \(\mathbb Q_7\) of degree \(r\), and let \(\operatorname{Tr}_r:\mathcal O_r\to\mathbb Z_7\) be its trace. For \(t\in\mathbb F_{7^r}\), write \([t]\) for its Teichmüller lift: \([0]=0\), and for \(t\ne0\), \([t]\) is the unique \((7^r-1)\)-st root of unity reducing to \(t\). Define the convergent Witt-ring-valued function
\[
 f_r(t)=[t]^{11}+\sum_{j=2}^{\infty}7^j[t]^{11\cdot7^j-19}.
\]
For each integer \(n\geq1\), choose a primitive \(7^n\)-th root of unity \(\zeta_{7^n}\in\mathbb C_7\), and define \(\chi_n:\mathbb Z_7\to\mathbb C_7^\times\) by \(\chi_n(z)=\zeta_{7^n}^{\,z\bmod7^n}\). Set
\[
 L_n(s)=\exp\!\left(\sum_{r=1}^{\infty}\frac{s^r}{r}\sum_{t\in\mathbb F_{7^r}}\chi_n\!\left(\operatorname{Tr}_r(f_r(t))\right)\right).
\]
For these data, \(L_n(s)\) is a polynomial. Define its characteristic series by the coefficientwise \(7\)-adically convergent product
\[
 C_n^*(s)=\prod_{j=0}^{\infty}(1-7^js)L_n(7^js)
          =\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}b_{n,k}s^k.
\]
Let \(N_n\) be the Newton polygon formed as the lower convex hull of
\[
 \bigl(k,\nu_n(b_{n,k})\bigr),\qquad k\in\mathbb Z_{\geq0},
 \qquad \nu_n=6\cdot7^{n-1}v_7,
\]
where the valuation of zero is \(+\infty\). Regard \(N_n(x)\) as the piecewise-linear ordinate of this polygon for real \(x\geq0\). Thus \(\nu_n(\zeta_{7^n}-1)=1\), and the factor \((1-s)\) is included in the polygon.

Define the adjacent-level agreement radius
\[
 \mathcal R_n=\sup\left\{R\geq0:\ N_n(x)=N_{n+1}(x)\text{ for every }x\in[0,R]\right\},
\]
with \(\mathcal R_n=+\infty\) when the two polygons agree on the entire half-line. Determine an explicit exact formula for \(\mathcal R_n\) for every integer \(n\geq1\).
</problem>

14	
15	## 1. A reference polygon
16	
17	Let \(P\) be the polygon with slopes
18	\[
19	0,\ \underbrace{3,\ldots,3}_{10},\
20	6,\ \underbrace{9,\ldots,9}_{10},\
21	12,\ \underbrace{15,\ldots,15}_{10},\ldots.
22	\]
23	Its vertices include
24	\[
25	\begin{aligned}
26	P(11m)&=33m^2-3m,\\
27	P(11m+1)&=33m^2+3m.
28	\end{aligned}                                                    \tag{1}
29	\]
30	For \(1\le r\le11\),
31	\[
32	P(11m+r)=33m^2+3m+(6m+3)(r-1).
33	\]
34	Put
35	\[
36	H(x)=\frac3{11}x(x-1).
37	\]
38	Then
39	\[
40	P(11m+r)-H(11m+r)=\frac{3(r-1)(11-r)}{11}.                         \tag{2}
41	\]
42	
43	We will show that every \(N_n\) differs from \(P\), if at all, only through possible coefficient points one unit below \(P\) at indices congruent to \(5\) or \(7\pmod {11}\).
44	
45	## 2. The Dwork determinant and its weights
46	
47	Write
48	\[
49	E(X)=\exp\left(\sum_{a\ge0}\frac{X^{7^a}}{7^a}\right)
50	     =\sum_{h\ge0}e_hX^h.
51	\]
52	We use \(e_h=0\) for \(h<0\). The Artin–Hasse integrality theorem gives \(e_h\in\mathbb Z_7\). For example, it follows from
53	\[
54	E(X)=\prod_{\substack{u\ge1\\7\nmid u}}
55	       (1-X^u)^{-\mu(u)/u}.
56	\]
57	
58	Fix a level \(n\). Choose \(\pi_j\), \(0\le j<n\), by
59	\[
60	E(\pi_j)=\zeta_{7^n}^{\,7^j}.
61	\]
62	Then
63	\[
64	\nu_n(\pi_j)=7^j,\qquad
65	\frac{\pi_j}{\pi_0^{7^j}}\equiv1\pmod{\pi_0}.                       \tag{3}
66	\]
67	Indeed, formal inversion of \(E(X)-1\), together with Frobenius modulo \(7\), gives
68	\(\pi_j\equiv\pi_0^{7^j}\pmod7\); here
69	\(\nu_n(7)>7^j\).
70	
71	Set \(d_j=11\cdot7^j-19\), and define
72	\[
73	F_n(X)=E(\pi_0X^{11})\prod_{j=2}^{n-1}E(\pi_jX^{d_j})
74	      =\sum_{h\ge0}\lambda_hX^h.
75	\]
76	The Dwork matrix is
77	\[
78	A_n=(\lambda_{7i-j})_{i,j\ge0}.
79	\]
80	The splitting lemma and trace formula give
81	\[
82	C_n^*(s)=\det(1-sA_n).                                             \tag{4}
83	\]
84	Here the determinant is the one for the multiplicative group, so its zero-index row and column include exactly the factor \((1-s)\) required in the question.
85	
86	For completeness, the normalization follows directly from the trace formula:
87	\[
88	\operatorname{Tr}(A_n^r)
89	 =\frac{1}{7^r-1}
90	   \sum_{t\in\mathbb F_{7^r}^{\times}}
91	     \chi_n(\operatorname{Tr}_r f_r(t)).
92	\]
93	Taking logarithms of (4) therefore gives the logarithm of the stated product defining \(C_n^*\).
94	
95	Consider a term in a principal minor indexed by a \(k\)-element set \(I\subseteq\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\). Let \(A\) denote the total number of factors selected from the splitting factors with \(j\ge2\), counted with multiplicity. Its valuation is at least
96	\[
97	w=\frac{6\sum_{i\in I}i+19A}{11}.                                  \tag{5}
98	\]
99	This follows by summing, over a determinant permutation,
100	\[
101	11a_0+\sum_{j\ge2}(11\cdot7^j-19)a_j=7i-\sigma(i).
102	\]
103	The quantity in (5) is an integer whenever such a term exists.
104	
105	### Terms with \(A=0\)
106	
107	Such terms require the multiplicities of the nonzero residue classes of \(I\pmod {11}\) to be equal: multiplication by \(7\) acts transitively on the ten nonzero residues modulo \(11\).
108	
109	If their common multiplicity is \(a\), and the multiplicity of residue zero is \(b\), then
110	\[
111	k=10a+b,\qquad
112	w\ge30a^2+3b(b-1).                                                 \tag{6}
113	\]
114	The lower convex hull of these bounds is precisely \(P\). One way to see this is to merge the two lists of incremental costs:
115	\[
116	0,6,12,\ldots
117	\quad\text{and}\quad
118	\underbrace{3,\ldots,3}_{10},
119	\underbrace{9,\ldots,9}_{10},\ldots.
120	\]
121	Thus \(A=0\) terms cannot lie below \(P\).
122	
123	### Terms with \(A>0\)
124	
125	Put
126	\[
127	\delta=\sum_{i\in I}i-\frac{k(k-1)}2\ge0.
128	\]
129	Equations (2) and (5) show that a term below \(P\), with \(k=11m+r\), must satisfy
130	\[
131	6\delta+19A<3(r-1)(11-r),\qquad
132	3r(r-1)+6\delta+19A\equiv0\pmod {11}.                              \tag{7}
133	\]
134	The right side of the inequality is at most \(75\), so \(A\le3\).
135	
136	There is one more necessary condition: the residue multiplicities must admit the determinant matching. A base-factor edge sends row residue \(a\) to column residue \(7a\), while a factor counted \(b\) times from the other splitting factors sends it to \(7a-3b\).
137	
138	Checking these finite conditions gives the following complete table. “Admissible sets” means sets satisfying this necessary residue-matching condition.
139	
140	\[
141	\begin{array}{c|c|c|c}
142	r&A&\delta&\text{number of admissible sets}\\ \hline
143	3&1&3&0\\
144	4&1&0&0\\
145	5&1&7&1\\
146	5&2&2&0\\
147	6&1&2&0\\
148	7&1&7&1\\
149	7&2&2&0\\
150	8&1&0&0\\
151	9&1&3&0
152	\end{array}                                                       \tag{8}
153	\]
154	There are no other solutions of (7). The two surviving sets are
155	\[
156	\begin{aligned}
157	I_5(m)&=\{0,\ldots,11m-1\}
158	        \cup\{11m,11m+2,11m+3,11m+5,11m+7\},\\
159	I_7(m)&=\{0,\ldots,11m-1\}
160	        \cup\{11m,11m+1,11m+2,11m+3,11m+5,11m+7,11m+10\}.
161	\end{aligned}                                                     \tag{9}
162	\]
163	In both cases (5) equals \(P(k)-1\).
164	
165	The enumeration in (8) involves only partitions of \(\delta\le7\). The code below checks it exhaustively, including the boundary case \(m=0\). Its independence of \(m\ge1\) follows by translating the altered final indices by \(11\).
166	
167	Consequently,
168	\[
169	\nu_n(b_{n,k})\ge P(k),
170	\]
171	except possibly at \(k=11m+5,11m+7\), where the lower bound is \(P(k)-1\). Whether that exceptional value occurs is decided by one coefficient in \(\mathbb F_7\).
172	
173	## 3. Contact points and elementary determinant identities
174	
175	We need that the points in (1) are genuine contact points.
176	
177	For \(0\le c\le6\), define
178	\[
179	D_{m,c}=\det(e_{7i-j+c})_{0\le i,j<m}.
180	\]
181	Since \(E(X)=\exp(X)G(X^7)\), multiplication by \(G(X^7)\) performs a lower-unitriangular transformation on these rows. Therefore
182	\[
183	D_{m,c}
184	=\det\left(\frac1{(7i-j+c)!}\right)_{0\le i,j<m}
185	=\frac{7^{m(m-1)/2}\prod_{i=1}^{m-1}i!}
186	       {\prod_{i=0}^{m-1}(7i+c)!}.                                 \tag{10}
187	\]
188	The last equality is the falling-factorial Vandermonde determinant. Legendre’s formula shows that the numerator and denominator have equal \(7\)-adic valuation. Thus every \(D_{m,c}\) is a \(7\)-adic unit.
189	
190	At \(k=11m,11m+1\), the unique smallest-weight index set is
191	\(\{0,\ldots,k-1\}\). Its base-factor determinant splits, by residues modulo \(11\), into determinants (10). It follows that
192	\[
193	N_n(11m)=P(11m),\qquad N_n(11m+1)=P(11m+1).                         \tag{11}
194	\]
195	They are indeed polygon contact points, since all coefficient points lie on or above the strictly convex quadratic \(H\).
196	
197	In particular,
198	\[
199	P(x)-1\le N_n(x)\le P(x),                                         \tag{12}
200	\]
201	and the polygon within each interval
202	\([11m+1,11m+11]\) is completely determined by the two possible lowered points in (9).
203	
204	## 4. How a newly appearing term first affects the polygon
205	
206	For \(I_5(m)\), the only possible nonbase edge goes from residue \(3\) to residue \(7\). For \(I_7(m)\), it goes from residue \(10\) to residue \(1\).
207	
208	After grouping rows and columns by residues, the relevant rectangular blocks are as follows:
209	\[
210	\begin{array}{c|ccc}
211	r&U_{\ell h}&V_{\ell h}&B_j{}_{\ell h}\\ \hline
212	5&e_{7\ell-h+1}&e_{7\ell-h}&e_{7\ell-h+3-7^j}\\
213	7&e_{7\ell-h+6}&e_{7\ell-h+5}&e_{7\ell-h+8-7^j}.
214	\end{array}                                                       \tag{13}
215	\]
216	Here \(U\) has size \((m+1)\times m\), \(V\) has size \(m\times(m+1)\), and \(B_j\) has size \((m+1)\times(m+1)\). All the other blocks are square determinants of the form (10).
217	
218	The exceptional leading coefficient is, up to a common nonzero factor, the cofactor contraction
219	\[
220	u^{\!T}\left(\sum_{j=2}^{n-1}B_j\right)v,                          \tag{14}
221	\]
222	where \(u^TU=0\) and \(Vv=0\). Formula (3) is why all summands have coefficient \(1\) after reduction modulo the uniformizer.
223	
224	Now compare levels \(n\) and \(n+1\), and put
225	\[
226	M=7^{n-1}.
227	\]
228	The new summand is \(B_n\).
229	
230	For \(r=5\), it is zero whenever
231	\[
232	7m+3<7^n,
233	\]
234	hence whenever \(m<M\). For \(r=7\), it is zero whenever
235	\[
236	7m+8<7^n,
237	\]
238	hence whenever \(m<M-1\).
239	
240	Thus the two polygons have identical exceptional-point decisions in every block \(m<M-1\). By (11),
241	\[
242	N_n(x)=N_{n+1}(x)
243	\quad\text{for }0\le x\le11M-10.                                  \tag{15}
244	\]
245	
246	At the critical block \(m=M-1\), the new \(r=5\) matrix is still zero. The new \(r=7\) matrix has just two nonzero entries:
247	\[
248	(B_n)_{m,0}=e_1=1,\qquad (B_n)_{m,1}=e_0=1.                       \tag{16}
249	\]
250	
251	This gives a **nonzero** change in the exceptional leading coefficient. Here are the details, including the possible cancellation between the two entries.
252	
253	Choose the cofactor normalizations
254	\[
255	u_m=D_{m,6},\qquad
256	v_0=D_{m,4},\qquad
257	v_1=-\det(e_{7i-h+5})_{\substack{0\le i<m\\h\in\{0,2,\ldots,m\}}}.
258	\]
259	The same lower-triangular row argument used in (10), followed by a Vandermonde calculation, gives
260	\[
261	v_0+v_1
262	=D_{m,4}\prod_{\ell=0}^{m-1}\frac{7\ell+4}{7\ell+5}.               \tag{17}
263	\]
264	Every factor on the right is a unit.
265	
266	For clarity, the Vandermonde calculation in (17) is especially simple. Set \(x_\ell=7\ell+5\) and factor \(1/x_\ell!\) from row \(\ell\). The first column in \(v_0+v_1\) is
267	\((x_\ell)_1-(x_\ell)_0=x_\ell-1\); the remaining columns are
268	\((x_\ell)_2,\ldots,(x_\ell)_m\). Factoring \(x_\ell-1\) from each row leaves monic polynomials of degrees \(0,\ldots,m-1\). For \(v_0\), the corresponding row factor is \(x_\ell\). Their ratio is precisely the product in (17).
269	
270	Equations (16)–(17) show that the new contribution is
271	\[
272	u_m(v_0+v_1)\ne0\pmod7.                                           \tag{18}
273	\]
274	
275	It remains to show that the old polygon is straight in this critical block. This is where duality enters.
276	
277	## 5. The old polygon is straight in its final block
278	
279	Write
280	\[
281	e_n=6\cdot7^{n-1}.
282	\]
283	
284	We use the standard reciprocal-root duality for additive-character \(L\)-functions on \(\mathbb A^1\):
285	if the normalized valuations of the reciprocal roots of \(L_n\) are \(\alpha_i\), their multiset is invariant under
286	\[
287	\alpha\longmapsto e_n-\alpha.                                    \tag{19}
288	\]
289	
290	Here is why it applies, without any slope-stability assumption. The finite Witt expression defining the level-\(n\) character gives an Artin–Schreier–Witt cover of \(\mathbb A^1\). It is geometrically connected because its first equation has right side \(x^{11}\), which is not an Artin–Schreier coboundary. It is ramified only at infinity, and its inertia group there is the full cyclic group. Thus the nontrivial character part of the first cohomology of its smooth projective completion has characteristic polynomial \(L_n\). Poincaré duality pairs the character and inverse-character parts, taking reciprocal roots \(\beta\) to \(7/\beta\). The inverse-character polynomial is obtained by \(\zeta_{7^n}\mapsto\zeta_{7^n}^{-1}\), an automorphism preserving \(v_7\). This proves (19).
291	
292	We can obtain the degree needed below directly from the determinant estimates, without invoking a ramification-degree formula. If \(D=\deg L_n\), the product defining \(C_n^*\) has slopes consisting of \(D+1\) fixed slopes and all their translates by \(je_n\). Hence its quadratic asymptotic is
293	\[
294	N_n(x)=\frac{e_n}{2(D+1)}x^2+O(x).
295	\]
296	On the other hand, (12) gives leading coefficient \(3/11\). Therefore
297	\[
298	D+1=11\cdot7^{n-1}.                                               \tag{20}
299	\]
300	
301	The first eleven slopes of \(N_n\) are \(0,3,\ldots,3\). Indeed, (13) has no nonzero \(B_j\) in the first block, since \(j\ge2\). Consequently all reciprocal roots of \(L_n\) have positive valuation. Duality (19) then puts them strictly below \(e_n\).
302	
303	It follows from (20) that the first \(11M\) slopes of \(C_n^*\) are exactly
304	\[
305	0,\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_{11M-1}.
306	\]
307	For \(n\ge2\), its first ten nonzero slopes are \(3\), so its last ten slopes in this period are \(e_n-3\), by (19). Using the contact point at \(11M\), we obtain
308	\[
309	N_n(x)=P(x)\qquad(11M-10\le x\le11M).                             \tag{21}
310	\]
311	
312	In particular, the old exceptional leading coefficient at \(k=11M-4\) is zero. By (18), the new one is nonzero. Thus
313	\[
314	\nu_{n+1}(b_{n+1,\,11M-4})=P(11M-4)-1.
315	\]
316	The new polygon consequently lies strictly below \(P\) immediately to the right of the common contact point \(11M-10\). Together with (15) and (21), this proves
317	\[
318	\mathcal R_n=11M-10\qquad(n\ge2).
319	\]
320	
321	At levels \(1\) and \(2\), no factors with \(j\ge2\) occur at all. Only the \(A=0\) calculation applies, and (11) forces
322	\[
323	N_1=N_2=P.
324	\]
325	Therefore \(\mathcal R_1=+\infty\), completing the proof.
326	
327	## 6. Executable checks
328	
329	The following Python does actual finite computations:
330	
331	* exhaustively checks table (8);
332	* checks the exact determinant identities, not merely their valuations;
333	* computes the exceptional coefficients over \(\mathbb F_7\);
334	* constructs and compares the relevant polygon blocks;
335	* independently finds the first differing blocks for \(n=2,3\).
336	
337	It requires NumPy and SymPy.
338	
339	```python
340	from fractions import Fraction
341	from math import factorial
342	import numpy as np
343	import sympy as sp
344	
345	
346	def partitions(n, lo=1):
347	    if n == 0:
348	        yield ()
349	    for a in range(lo, n + 1):
350	        for tail in partitions(n - a, a):
351	            yield (a,) + tail
352	
353	
354	def index_sets(k, delta):
355	    for part in partitions(delta):
356	        if len(part) > k:
357	            continue
358	        I = list(range(k))
359	        for j, a in enumerate(part):
360	            I[k - len(part) + j] += a

372	        return out

376	        if np.array_equal(difference, edge(a, A)):
377	            options.append((a, A))
